But all this leaves us with a yet-unanswered question: where does the video game industry go from here? To that end, I reached out to two very relevant figures for answers: Dr Luke Dicken, Take-Twoâs former head of artificial intelligence, and Emilio Coppola, Godot Engineâs executive director.

Given his work experience, Dicken is an especially pertinent man to interview on the topic. Starting in 2019, he served as Zynga’s director of applied AI before becoming its senior director of applied AI in 2022. âThis new wave of decompile-and-port is definitely something that developers and publishers need to take seriously,â stated Dicken. âIt strikes me as noteworthy that this is being enabled by the subsidization of GenAI costs by the frontier labs, so this is an artificially enlarged problem right now, but it’s not one that’s going away, even if it might reduce in scale when the AI bubble pops.â

Hearing someone in Dickenâs line of work state that the AI bubble popping is a matter of âwhen,â opposed to âif,â may astonish you. However, he took a similar stance in a recent interview with PocketGamerbiz .

Dicken told me that he believes âwe could see more of a push towards systems of protecting the gamesâ that are now threatened by AIâs sudden ability to decompile source code. Dicken stated that, as many have already theorized, said systems âwill probably be consumer-hostile in an effort to combat this sort of thing.â That means âmore invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.â

Emilio Coppolaâs opinion on the subject is relevant for very different reasons. Coppola is the executive director of Godot Engine and the founder of its non-profit organization, the Godot Foundation. Even if youâve not heard of Godot Engine, youâve almost definitely heard of many of the games that utilize it, as it’s the open-source game engine behind the likes of Slay the Spire II , Brotato , Buckshot Roulette , and Dome Keeper .

Coppolaâs stance on the recent evolution of AI coding was similarly negative, although he was far more concerned with the platforms that are âenablingâ the âbad actorsâ who utilize said advancements to thrive. But which platforms is Coppola referring to here? Primarily, Steam.

While Coppola stated that he believes âa developer has very little ways of protecting themselves in today’s climate,â he noted that this âwas also the caseâ before Opus 5.5, specifically in reference to video game piracy. However, he asserted that âthe main differenceâ when it comes to recent AI coding advancements âis that people are making a profit out of it.â

â[The] burden shouldn’t fall on the developers to protect their games against bad actors,â stated Coppola. âThe burden should fall onto the platforms who are enabling this sort of behavior. A platform like Steam is profiting and allowing bad actors to sell low-quality clones of a project that a developer worked on, yet they never get the blame.â

The âbad actorsâ Coppola is referring to here are the people producing AI vibe-coded ripoffs of indie games . Said ripoffs are then repackaged under extremely similar names and subsequently published on Steam. Dickenâs thoughts on the matter echoed Coppolaâs, as he told me that âAI is empowering people to do things at an unprecedented scaleâboth for good and ill.â

âRipping off someone else’s games, cracking games, decompiling them…none of these are new behaviors, but they are now more easily accessed and happening much more broadly,â continued Dicken. âOur defensive structuresâsocial, legal, and technicalâare all lagging behind, but I think over time there’s going to be a stabilization. I hope.â

Of course, this isnât the first time weâve heard about the Godot Engine in relation to vibe-coding. Back in February, Godot Engineâs project manager, RÃ©mi Verschelde, bemoaned the wave of âAI slopâ pull requests on Godotâs GitHub . Eventually, in July, the maintainers of Godotâs GitHub decided they’d had enough. A new rule was then added to its contribution policy : âWe require all code to be human authored.â

I asked Coppola if the arrival of Claude Opus 5.5 had made Godotâs vibe-coding problem on GitHub worse. He said that he didnât believe its decompiling capabilities had âaffected Godot at all,â as Godotâs engine has always been âpublic and open source.â

However, Coppola believes it may have affected Godotâs developers in a different way entirely, as heâs heard that âmany developersâ are now too âworried and anxious to even share early-access versions of their games,â as there is suddenly a ârisk of it being cloned by somebody else.â

There are, unfortunately, lots of examples we could pull from here to illustrate Coppolaâs point, but one such example is especially applicable: on October 7, a DMCA request from Mega Crit, the publishers and developers behind Slay the Spire II , was processed on GitHub. It states that an infringing GitHub page contained Slay the Spire IIâs âproprietary source code, which has never been published or licensed for public distribution.â

However, to leave us on a more hopeful note, Dicken and Coppola also agreed on one specific front: while AIâs capability to produce and iterate code may have drastically improved, both assured me that they feel it can never replace the creative capabilities of the video game industryâs talented developers.

While Dicken stated that we may have already found ourselves âin a world where ideas and execution are cheap,â how developers and publishers choose to âoperateâ their games and their businesses will be the âcore differentiatorsâ moving forward: âAI can clone a game, it can decompile an existing thing and repurpose it, but what it can’t do is find the fun of the next thing. That’s still a uniquely human endeavor.â

Likewise, although Coppola noted that some âmight benefitâ from the recent âadvancementsâ of AI coding, he also stated that âcoding is rarely the roadblock in making a successful game,â and that âgood game designâ will always endure: âHaving good game design and basically âsomething that’s fun,â it’s really difficult to do, no matter if you are the one coding or if it’s a robot doing it.
